text: Every year America marks National Doctors' Day on March 30th,
visual: Tear-off calendar flips to March 30 for National Doctors' Day.

text: and most people have no idea why it's that date,
visual: Kinetic card asks the question the narration just asked.

text: and the reason is a country doctor in Georgia
visual: Map flies in to Georgia; a pin drops on Jefferson.

text: named Crawford Long, who on March 30th, 1842,

text: put a man under ether and took a tumor off his neck.

text: But the famous moment in the history of anesthesia, the one in the textbooks,

text: and I don't mean the gory part, I mean what doctors actually believed.
visual: Compare card: not the gory part, but what doctors believed.

text: Before anesthesia, many doctors didn't think pain was purely a bad thing,

steps.label: A sign the body was still fighting

visual: Flow: first box, many doctors didn't think pain was purely a bad thing.

text: some saw it as a sign the body was still fighting,

steps.label: A sign the body was still fighting

visual: Flow: second box, some saw it as a sign the body was still fighting.

text: and some opposed anesthesia because they thought taking away the pain could be dangerous.

fields.headline: Some opposed anesthesia
fields.sub: They thought taking away the pain could be dangerous

visual: Kinetic card carrying the hedge "some".

text: And that wasn't just a few cranks, the great French physiologist François Magendie

fields.lower: François Magendie, the French physiologist (lithograph by N. E. Maurin)

text: argued that pain, in his words, "has always its usefulness."
visual: Typewriter quote: Magendie's own words.

text: A peer-reviewed medical review calls it an "erroneous yet pervasive Western view,"
visual: Typewriter quote from the medical review.

text: the idea that the patient's anguish was part of what kept them alive.

steps.label: Part of what kept them alive

visual: Flow: the patient's anguish, then part of what kept them alive.
